cues.text: Welcome to Chemical Kinetics.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Kinetics asks how quickly a reaction proceeds.
Equilibrium asks about its preferred composition.
A thermodynamically favourable reaction can still be slow.
Average rate describes a finite interval; instantaneous rate is the local
slope
of the concentration time curve.
For two A forming B at constant volume, A disappears twice as quickly as B
forms.
Divide the disappearance rate of A by its coefficient two to obtain the
normalized reaction rate.
If A disappears at zero point zero four zero molar per second, the reaction
rate is zero point zero two zero molar per second.
Read whether the question asks for a species rate or the normalized rate.
Now determine a rate law from experiments.
Our first experiment uses A and B concentrations each zero point one zero
molar
and gives rate zero point zero zero two zero molar per second.
In the second, only A doubles and the rate quadruples.
The exponent of A is therefore two.
In the third, only B doubles and the rate doubles.
Its exponent is one.
The law is k times A squared times B, with total order three.
Do not copy those exponents from an overall chemical equation; they are
experimental results.
Substitute the first row to find k.
Divide zero point zero zero two zero by zero point one squared times zero
point
one.
The result is two point zero, with units molar to the minus two per second.
At unchanged temperature and conditions, tripling A and halving B changes rate
by nine times one half, or four point five.
Each concentration ratio gets its own exponent.
Overall order three does not mean every mixed change gets cubed.
Order and molecularity answer different questions.
Total order is the sum of exponents in an empirical rate law.
It may be zero or fractional.
Molecularity counts reacting entities in a single elementary step and is a
positive integer.
Do not assign molecularity to an arbitrary multistep overall equation.
If rate uses concentration per time and total order is r, the units of k are
concentration to the power one minus r, divided by time.
A first order k has inverse time units.
A zero order k has concentration per time units.
For an order of one half, k has concentration to the one half per time.
Units are a useful check, not a substitute for reading the experiment.
For zero order disappearance, the concentration decreases by a fixed amount
per
unit time while the model holds.
Integrating gives concentration at time t equals initial concentration minus k
times t.
A plot of concentration against time is straight with slope minus k.
Take initial concentration zero point zero eight zero zero molar and k zero
point zero zero two zero zero molar per minute.
After fifteen minutes the loss is zero point zero three zero zero molar,
leaving zero point zero five zero zero.
Setting concentration to zero gives depletion time forty minutes.
Extrapolating beyond that would predict a negative concentration and is
physically invalid.
The zero order half life is initial concentration divided by two k.
Here it is twenty minutes.
Doubling the initial concentration doubles that half life at the same k.
A zero order description can apply over a limited range, such as a saturated
catalyst surface.
State its valid range rather than assuming that the same straight line governs
every possible concentration.
For first order disappearance, the rate is proportional to the amount still
present.
Equal time intervals remove equal fractions rather than equal amounts.
The integrated law is the natural logarithm of initial concentration divided
by
remaining concentration equals k times t.
The ratio inside the logarithm is dimensionless.
The half life is natural log two divided by k and is independent of the
starting concentration in this model.
Suppose the half life is ten minutes.
Thirty minutes is three half lives, so the fraction remaining is one half
cubed, or one eighth.
That is twelve point five percent remaining, not twelve point five percent
consumed.
For ninety percent completion, ten percent remains.
Calculate k as natural log two divided by ten, about zero point zero six nine
three one per minute.
The required time is natural log ten divided by k, about thirty three point
two
minutes.
Never replace percent remaining by percent consumed inside the logarithm.
Here is another check.
A reactant is seventy five percent consumed in twenty minutes.
One quarter remains, so two half lives have elapsed and each half life is ten
minutes.
To reach ninety three point seven five percent consumption, one sixteenth must
remain.
That is four half lives in total, or forty minutes.
The additional time after the first observation is twenty minutes.
A plot of natural log concentration against time is straight with slope minus
k, using a consistent concentration reference.
Finally, keep the time unit consistent.
A k value of zero point one two zero per minute equals zero point zero zero
two
zero zero per second.
Multiplying an inverse minute constant by a time in seconds without conversion
gives the wrong decay.
Pressure measurements can reveal a rate constant, but only after stoichiometry
connects pressure to the reactant.
Assume initially pure ideal gas A decomposes to one B plus one C.
Temperature and volume stay constant, and no other gases or reactions are
present.
Let the reacted fraction be f.
Starting with n zero moles, the remaining A is n zero times one minus f.
The amounts of B and C are each n zero f.
Total moles are therefore n zero times one plus f.
At fixed temperature and volume, total pressure divided by initial pressure
equals one plus f.
If the initial pressure is one hundred kilopascals and the total pressure
after
ten minutes is one hundred fifty, f is one half.
Remaining A has partial pressure fifty kilopascals.
Equivalently, A's partial pressure is twice the initial pressure minus the
current total pressure.
Use that partial pressure in the first order disappearance law, because it is
proportional to A concentration under the stated conditions.
k equals natural log of one hundred divided by fifty, all divided by ten
minutes.
The answer is about zero point zero six nine three per minute.
Total pressure rises because one reactant molecule produces two product
molecules, while the amount of A falls.
Directly inserting total pressure into a disappearance formula would give the
wrong sign.
Check the limiting pressures.
At the beginning, total pressure is one hundred.
At complete conversion it approaches two hundred in this model.
If the reaction stoichiometry, initial mixture, temperature or volume changes,
derive a new pressure relation.
Do not memorize twice initial minus total as a universal gas kinetics formula.
The reliable method is a mole balance followed by the ideal gas relation.
The Arrhenius model writes k as A times the exponential of minus activation
energy divided by R T.
Use temperature in kelvin and match the energy units of activation energy and
R.
If A is approximately constant and activation energy is positive, higher
temperature increases k.
Comparing two temperatures gives natural log of k two over k one equals
activation energy over R, multiplied by one over T one minus one over T two.
Suppose k doubles between three hundred and three hundred ten kelvin.
Use R equal to eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin.
Activation energy is R times natural log two, divided by one over three
hundred
minus one over three hundred ten.
The result is about fifty three thousand six hundred joules per mole, or fifty
three point six kilojoules per mole.
The sign is positive, as expected.
A plot of natural log k against inverse temperature has slope minus activation
energy over R.
There is no universal rule that every ten degree rise doubles every reaction
rate.
In elementary collision theory for gaseous bimolecular reactions, encounters
need sufficient energy and suitable orientation.
Counting all collisions as successful would overestimate the reaction rate.
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower effective activation
barrier and speeds the approach to equilibrium.
At unchanged temperature it does not change the equilibrium constant or the
reaction enthalpy.
It may participate in intermediate steps without being consumed in the net
reaction.
Finish each kinetics problem by identifying the rate definition, selecting the
order and model, converting units, and checking physical limits.
Use the twelve original practice questions and the seven worked examples in
the notes.
This recording covers the core foundation of Unit eight; broader experimental
datasets and mechanism practice remain useful.
The questions are original practice, not official past papers.
A reaction rate and a species disappearance rate are not always the same
number.
For the balanced decomposition of two moles of dinitrogen pentoxide into four
moles of nitrogen dioxide and one mole of oxygen, divide each concentration
slope by its stoichiometric coefficient.
Suppose dinitrogen pentoxide disappears at zero point zero zero four zero
moles
per litre per second at constant volume.
The normalized forward reaction rate is half that value, zero point zero zero
two zero.
Nitrogen dioxide appears four times as fast as the normalized rate, giving
zero
point zero zero eight zero.
Oxygen appears at zero point zero zero two zero.
All three statements describe the same reaction progress.
The negative sign in a disappearance derivative makes the forward rate
positive; it does not mean the concentration is negative.
These coefficient relationships follow from stoichiometry, while experimental
concentration exponents in a rate law are a different matter.
If volume changes substantially, account for that change before identifying a
concentration derivative with a simple molar production rate.
Read exactly which species and which definition the question requests.
A reaction can appear first order when one concentration remains nearly
constant.
Consider an experimentally established disappearance law for A equal to k
times
A concentration times B concentration.
If B is present in very large excess, consuming A changes B only slightly
over the measurement interval.
Combine k and the effectively constant B concentration into an observed first
order constant.
With k equal to zero point zero two zero litres per mole per second and B
concentration zero point five zero moles per litre, the observed constant is
zero point zero one zero per second.
The predicted half life of A is about sixty nine point three seconds.
The original constant still has second order units, while the observed
constant
has inverse time units.
Doubling the maintained B concentration doubles the observed constant and
halves that half life within the model.
This does not turn the underlying overall order into a universal first order
law.
If B is depleted significantly, the approximation fails.
In ester hydrolysis examples, solvent and catalyst conditions must also be
controlled rather than silently absorbed into an unexplained constant.
Graph selection can distinguish an amount removed from a fraction removed.
Under zero order disappearance, concentration itself decreases linearly with
time and the slope is minus the zero order constant.
For first order disappearance, the natural logarithm of the remaining
concentration divided by its initial value is linear, with slope minus the
first order constant.
Using the ratio keeps the logarithm dimensionless.
Equal successive half lives support a first order model; a half life
proportional to starting concentration supports zero order over its applicable
range.
Suppose a first order logarithmic plot has slope minus zero point zero three
zero per minute.
The constant is positive zero point zero three zero per minute and half life
is
about twenty three point one minutes.
A straight concentration plot with slope minus zero point zero zero three zero
moles per litre per minute instead has a zero order constant with
concentration
per time units.
Do not compare those numerical slopes as if their units matched.
A good fit over a narrow interval is evidence for a model, not proof of an
elementary mechanism.
A completion percentage must be converted into the fraction still present.
For a first order reactant with a ten minute half life, seventy five percent
completion leaves one quarter, requiring two half lives or twenty minutes.
Eighty seven point five percent completion leaves one eighth, requiring thirty
minutes.
Ninety nine point nine percent completion leaves one thousandth, not nine
hundred ninety nine thousandths.
Its time is the natural logarithm of one thousand divided by the constant.
Since the constant is the natural logarithm of two divided by ten minutes, the
time is about ninety nine point seven minutes.
Thus nearly ten half lives are needed, even though the final amount is very
small.
Exact one hundred percent completion would require the logarithm of an
infinite
concentration ratio in this ideal continuous model; it has no finite predicted
time.
Real measurements have detection limits and the model may cease to apply at
very low concentrations.
For the same first order law, the ratio of ninety percent completion time to
half life is the natural logarithm of ten divided by the natural logarithm of
two.
An energy profile separates a barrier from the energy difference between
products and reactants.
In an illustrative single barrier enthalpy diagram, set reactants at zero and
products at minus thirty kilojoules per mole.
An uncatalysed peak at plus eighty gives a forward barrier of eighty and a
reverse barrier of one hundred ten.
The reverse barrier is measured upward from the lower product level, not from
zero.
If an alternative catalytic path has a peak at plus sixty with the same
endpoints, its forward and reverse barriers are sixty and ninety.
Both decrease, while the reaction enthalpy remains minus thirty.
A real catalytic mechanism can contain several intermediates and barriers;
this
simple diagram illustrates the bookkeeping.
The catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature,
although it can change how quickly equilibrium is approached.
Barrier differences alone do not guarantee a numerical rate ratio unless the
relevant prefactors and kinetic model are also specified.
Keep potential energy sketches, thermodynamic direction and experimentally
measured rates distinct.
